newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's leaking river, now a river of fire.
newsitem.headline: Australia's leaking river, now a river of fire.

text.p: In fact, the Cataract River southwest of Sydney frequently disappears after water leaks through cracks in the riverbed caused by underground coal mining.
Up to 1.5 million litres (330,000 gallons) a day is leaking, Tony Ross, spokesman for a government-appointed environmental committee for the river, told Reuters on Wednesday.
The leakage, coupled with high demand for drinking water by the city of Sydney and drought, caused the free flowing lower parts of the river to run dry in late 1996 and 1995, Ross said.
Local resident David Andrewartha told Reuters it takes six weeks for the lower reaches of the Cataract, which flows through deep gorges creating large pools, to run dry after a big storm.

A six-month experiment that has increased water flow from an upstream dam to compensate for the leaking has resulted in the Cataract again flowing -- but the water will be cut off at the end of July for scientists to see if it again leaks away.
Meanwhile, the unhappy river now faces another problem -- it bursts into flames if a lit match is thrown on it.
Inflammable methane gas escaping through the cracks in the riverbed, bubble to the surface and can be ignited with a match.
"Some of the larger bubbles belch like a geyser," Ross said.
Studies of the gas leaks, which started a few months ago, found the methane gas emissions equal that produced by 100 dairy cows, said a mine spokeswoman.
Australia's largest company, the Broken Hill Pty Ltd (BHP), which operates the local coal mine, said a government scientific report found 2,200 litres of methane an hour was being released.
The scientists found the methane was naturally occurring in the region's sandstone rock and not coming from the coal mine.

"Now, I don't know what 100 diary cows smell like, but there are hundreds and hundreds of these emissions. It stinks down there," said Andrewartha, adding that he has ignited the river, causing flames 1.2 metre (four feet) high.
Andrewartha said the gas was also leaking from the riverbank, causing the ground to heat up to around 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) and killing trees.
Ross, chairman of the Upper Nepean River Catchment Trust, said the gas bubbles only occurred along a small section of the narrow, winding river.
"Nobody seems to know how to fix it," Ross said.
"The real danger is unaware visitors lighting matches and setting fire to themselves and scrub."
